newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Armenia rejects OSCE criticism of poll.
newsitem.headline: Armenia rejects OSCE criticism of poll.

text.p: Armenian authorities on Thursday rejected a charge by international observers that serious irregularities during last month's presidential election could call into question President Levon Ter-Petrosyan's victory.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) issued a report saying there were "very serious breaches" of election law in voting on September 22 and the ballot count, which showed Ter-Petrosyan had beaten rival Vazgen Manukyan.
Armenian electoral commission chairman Khachik Bezirjyan said the report was "misleading."
"We hope a new statement will be issued soon to dispell the suspicion created by these inaccuracies and minimize the damage," he told reporters on Thursday.
Ter-Petrosyan's office earlier angrily rebutted the OSCE charges, saying the observers, led by Briton Simon Osborn, had got their sums wrong.

"Because Osborn's reservations have arithmetical inaccuracies, the chairman of the Central Electoral Commission has sent a letter to the OSCE which corrects the figures that do not correspond to reality," said a spokesman.
Petrosyan, an aloof 51-year-old academic cleared the 50 percent hurdle by only 21,941 votes out of over 1.2 million valid ballots cast to capture a first-round win.

Manukyan's supporters protested against the result, storming parliament and clashing with police. Ter-Petrosyan, who has ruled Armenia since it broke from the Soviet Union in 1991, then sent tanks onto the streets and rounded up opposition activists.

"The OSCE/ODIHR International Observer Mission has concluded that very serious breaches in the election law took place during the vote tabulation process, the verification process and the aggregation of results, causing concern for the overall integrity of the election process," an OSCE statement said.

The report, issued to Reuters on Thursday in Warsaw by the OSCE's Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), was a strong condemnation for the OSCE, which ususally tempers its criticism of elections in emerging democracies.
The ODIHR said it was particularly concerned by a disparity of 22,013 between the number of people who voted and the number of voter coupons registered in the official results.

"Particularly given the fact...Ter-Petrosyan only passed the 50 percent threshold by 21,941 votes, the inaccuracies in the verification process can only contribute to a lack of confidence in the overall electoral process and could even question the results of the first round of balloting," it said.
The discrepancy was most marked in the capital Yerevan.
On Sunday Ter-Petrosyan was declared winner of the election with 51.8 percent of the vote, just above the level needed to avoid a runoff with Manukyan, a former prime minister who took 41.3 percent.
Manukyan, who has gone into hiding, has threatened to take the government to court over the alleged vote-rigging.

Diplomats and opposition politicians in Armenia, squeezed between Turkey, Iran, Azerbaijan and Georgia, have accused Ter-Petrosyan of using the opposition protests to jail opponents and stifle dissent. The president's aides reject the charges.

The OSCE said it would submit a final report shortly but urged a review of Armenia's election law to prevent future irregularities. "Clearly those who do not administer the law correctly should be sanctioned," it said.
